messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Architect
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Raj presents as a meticulously composed man, his professional success as a 41-year-old architect evident in his precise language and thoughtful demeanor. He is married and speaks of his wife, Priya, with a deep and gentle affection that contrasts sharply with the profound distress that has finally brought him to therapy. For the past decade, since the end of a previous relationship, he has been living with a private terror that has slowly eroded the foundations of his life.

The event itself occurred nearly twelve years ago, with his then-partner, Alex. Raj recalls the night not as a continuous narrative, but as a slideshow of stark, still images. Remembering it is like flipping through a series of photographs in his mind, each one bringing back the same wave of paralyzing fear he felt in the moment. There is the image of Alex’s face, contorted with rage, his words a slurred, incomprehensible torrent of sound. There is the sharp, botanical scent of gin on Alex’s breath as he screamed. There is a close-up of the pattern on their living room rug, seen from the floor after the first blow landed, the world spinning. And there is the memory of his own body, the nausea and dizziness that felt less like injury and more like a fundamental illness, a sickness from the inside out.

In the years that followed, these sensory fragments became tripwires in Raj’s daily life. The smell of alcohol is the most potent; walking past a bar or being near a colleague who had a drink at lunch can send a jolt of panic through him. This has made client dinners, a crucial part of his job, nearly impossible. He began making excuses, citing deadlines or feeling unwell, a pattern that has recently cost him a major project when he couldn't attend a key networking event. He came to believe he was failing in his most important role, not just as an architect, but as a provider. The chaotic sound of a busy construction site, with multiple conversations overlapping into an indistinct roar, mimics the auditory confusion of Alex’s rage, forcing Raj to delegate site visits he once enjoyed.

His body seems to hold its own memory of the threat. He describes how his body reacts to danger before he has even had time to think. A car backfiring on the street, a dish slipping from Priya’s hands in the kitchen—his muscles clench, his heart hammers against his ribs, and a cold sweat breaks out on his skin before his mind can even register the source of the sound. He feels perpetually jumpy, a coiled spring of anxiety. This state of high alert is most pronounced at night. Sleep offers no respite; instead, he finds himself lying awake for hours, convinced that he must stay vigilant, listening for any sound that might signal a threat. He feels an overwhelming need to protect the home he has built with Priya, a home he feels is constantly on the verge of being violated.

Underlying this constant state of alarm is a profound crisis of self. He was betrayed by someone he trusted completely, and this has shattered his ability to rely on his own judgment. He is plagued by a persistent self-doubt, a certainty that he can't trust himself to do the right thing, whether in a high-stakes design decision at his firm or a simple choice at home. This hesitation has made him seem indecisive and unreliable at work, further feeding his sense of failure. The trigger of feeling physically unwell is particularly insidious; a common head cold or a bout of indigestion is immediately interpreted by his body as the same sickness he felt on the floor that night, bringing with it a fresh surge of remembered terror. It was after missing a family gathering because of a minor stomach bug, and seeing the deep hurt in Priya’s eyes, that Raj finally decided he could no longer manage this alone. He is terrified of losing everything he has worked so hard to build since the assault, and he has come to therapy with the fragile hope of once again feeling safe in his own body and confident in his own mind.
